checkpoints: Monitoring and Observability are complements, not opposites — a CPU/RAM/latency dashboard is only half the story.
Monitoring covers known unknowns: you predefine which metrics to watch, compare them against a threshold, and fire an alert.
Monitoring's core question is always whether your SLIs (p95 latency, error rate, saturation) are meeting the SLOs you committed to.

Observability covers unknown unknowns: from metrics, logs, and traces emitted by the system, you infer its internal state to answer WHY it failed or drifted from expectations — even before any alert has had a chance to fire.

The classic blind spot is exactly what the teammate said: the aggregate dashboard stays all-green while users are still filing tickets, because the average smooths over a small fraction of broken requests (a localized failure hitting only one user segment or region) — the minority gets averaged away.
The fix is correlation: a metric flags "something is slow," and you pivot by trace_id from logs into traces to find exactly which hop is stalling.
You need both — Monitoring catches what you anticipated, Observability lets you debug what you never anticipated.
Centralize the logs so you query from one place, and index labels rather than full text, so that centralizing stays cheap.

In a microservice fleet, containers are ephemeral — they restart and get rescheduled onto other boxes, and their logs end up scattered everywhere, so SSHing into each box and grepping by hand collapses the moment there's more than a handful of services — you wouldn't even know which box still has the log.

A central label-indexed store solves the "one place to look" problem without paying full-text prices: it indexes only a small handful of low-cardinality labels — service, env — while the actual content is stored as compressed chunks it never tokenizes.
A full-text engine like Elasticsearch indexes every token in every line so you can search for any word anywhere, but running that at scale is expensive.

Label-indexing is orders of magnitude cheaper than full-text, at the cost of a filter-first workflow — you have to narrow by label (which service, which env) before you're allowed to line-scan or JSON-filter the content.

That workflow still supports per-request correlation: a trace_id lives inside the log content, not as a label, so you filter by service/env first, then search for that trace_id inside the narrowed stream — correlation stays cheap because you never had to full-text index the whole fleet to get it.

Consul's agent registration API only recognizes exact PascalCase field names (`ID`, `Name`, `Address`, `Port`); a payload sent with camelCase keys like `id`/`name`/`address`/`port` doesn't bind to those fields but isn't rejected either — the instance registers with an empty `Address` and zero `Port` while the register call still returns success with no error at all.
A service that registers with an empty address and port is still discoverable by name, so a consumer that looks it up gets back an entry that appears valid but cannot actually be connected to.

Omitting a `Check` block (an HTTP/TCP/TTL check with an `Interval`) from the registration payload leaves the registry with no independent way to detect that the instance has died, so a dead instance can sit in the catalog marked healthy indefinitely rather than for a single check cycle.

Without a `SIGTERM` handler that calls the deregister endpoint before the process exits, a normal rolling deploy or shutdown leaves a phantom entry in the service catalog, and every request routed to that entry in the meantime fails with connection refused.

A smoke test that boots exactly one instance and never kills it never queries discovery by name to inspect the returned address/port, never waits out a check interval, and never exercises a shutdown path — so it cannot surface field-casing, missing-health-check, or missing-deregister defects, all of which only show up under real production churn.

Verifying this kind of registration change requires querying discovery by service name and asserting the returned address/port are non-empty with a passing status, confirming a `Check` with an interval is actually configured, and then killing the instance to confirm its catalog entry disappears once deregister runs.

Field-casing mismatches against a registry API are silent failures because the API validates shape loosely and drops unrecognized keys instead of rejecting the request, which means code review — not a runtime error or a single-instance smoke test — is the only place this class of bug gets caught.

A monitoring backend stores one time series per unique combination of label values on a metric, not a single running count per metric name — so the number of stored series scales with the label key space, not with "how many requests happened."

Labels whose values only ever come from a small fixed set — an HTTP method, a route template, a status code — keep a counter's series count bounded no matter how much traffic arrives, because the same combinations just get incremented again.

A label whose value is unique per event — a freshly generated request UUID, or a per-user id — mints a brand-new time series on every single occurrence, so the series count grows without bound as traffic grows, eventually causing monitoring-backend RAM pressure, slow queries, scrape timeouts, and OOM.

Using the raw request path (e.g. `/users/123`) as a label instead of the route template (e.g. `/users/:id`) has the same unbounded effect as a user or request id, since every distinct resource id in the URL becomes its own series.

The fix is to shrink the counter's label set to only bounded values — method, a templated route, and status code — and drop the per-user and per-request labels from the metric entirely, using something like the middleware's own route-resolution helper to collapse concrete URLs into their template.

Removing an identity label from a metric does not sacrifice per-request debuggability: user id, request id, and trace id still belong in structured logs and distributed traces, which are built for high-cardinality, per-event detail in a way metrics are not — the two data types are meant to be tied together via a shared identifier like `trace_id` rather than merged into one.

The trade-off of this fix is honest, not free: you lose the ability to filter this exact user or request straight out of the metric itself, in exchange for the same forensic detail via a logs/traces lookup — a fair trade since metrics were never designed for per-event forensics.

The change can be verified by checking the monitoring backend's head series count (e.g. Prometheus's `numSeries`) before and after — confirming it stops climbing — and by checking that query p95/p99 latency and scrape duration return to normal budgets.

Exporting every trace with an always-on sampler is complete and safe for correctness, but at high traffic every span of every request gets built, batched, and shipped to the collector over OTLP — which is exactly what makes storage and bandwidth costs blow up.

A head sampler makes its keep/drop decision at the very first span of a trace, before any child span exists and before the request has even resolved, so the decision is made with zero knowledge of whether this trace will turn into an error or a slow outlier.

A flat random keep rate like 10% applies the same odds to every trace regardless of outcome, so it keeps 10% of the boring successes and only 10% of the rare errors and slow traces alike — throwing away roughly 90% of exactly the traces the team wants to retain.

Swapping the random sampler's percentage for a different fixed number does not fix the underlying problem, because the decision is still made at the same blind point in the pipeline before the trace's outcome is known.

The real fix is moving the keep/drop decision to after the trace's outcome is known: keep the SDK-side sampler as AlwaysOnSampler (or ParentBased(AlwaysOnSampler)) so nothing is dropped locally and every span still reaches the OpenTelemetry Collector.

A tail_sampling processor at the Collector buffers every span belonging to a trace until it completes, then applies an outcome-aware policy chain — always keep ERROR status, always keep p95-and-above latency, and only probabilistically sample a small percentage of the ordinary fast, successful traces.
This approach retains every error and slow trace by construction, discarding only the redundant 'everything was fine and fast' traces instead of discarding a random cross-section of everything.

Tail sampling trades storage savings for Collector memory and a buffering window, since it must hold all of a trace's spans until the trace completes or times out before it can decide, and it only produces correct decisions when every span of a given trace lands on the same Collector instance — which requires a load-balancing exporter keyed on traceId, otherwise the policy is evaluating an incomplete trace.
Standardize one JSON log shape across the whole fleet and get the label/content split right — that is the whole contract.

Every line carries: level, service, timestamp, message, and a correlation id — trace_id, ideally the same id the tracing pillar already generates, so one identifier ties a log line and a trace span to the same request.
The only fields promoted to indexed labels are the low-cardinality source descriptors: service, env, region — stable, small-value-set attributes that describe WHERE a log came from.
Everything that describes a specific request — trace_id, user_id, order_id — lives inside the content, never as a label.

The reason is cardinality: a label-indexed store opens a brand-new stream for every unique combination of label values, so a handful of services times a handful of envs stays a handful of streams, but promoting trace_id to a label means one new stream per request — millions of them — which crushes ingest throughput and turns every query into a scan across an exploded index.

Correlation still works without paying that cost: filter by label first (service=X, env=prod) to narrow down to the right stream, then line-filter or JSON-parse on trace_id inside that already-narrowed content to pull every line of one request across every service it touched.
None of this holds if it is left to each team's taste, so the contract is enforced fleet-wide through one shared logger configuration every service inherits, not a per-service reinvention.

It is deliberately narrower than the whole observability story: this contract covers operational logs only — it sits next to a separate error-tracking channel that captures unhandled exceptions with full stack traces, since logging one ERROR line is not the same as an exception actually reaching that channel.
Registration requires a logical Name — shared across instances of the same service, and exactly what a consumer discovers by, e.g. payment-service.
Registration also requires a unique instance ID, so the registry (and later a deregister call) can act on exactly one instance without disturbing its siblings that share the same Name.
Registration includes the network Address and Port the instance is actually reachable on.
A mandatory health Check (HTTP, TCP, or TTL) is required at registration — without one, a dead instance would sit in the catalog forever and discovery would keep handing it to consumers.

Lifecycle hooks: the instance self-registers on startup, and deregisters on SIGTERM so a graceful stop removes the catalog entry immediately — orchestrators like Kubernetes give a grace period specifically so this call lands before the container disappears.
Consumers must only ever be given instances currently passing their health check, never the full unfiltered catalog.

The interval/timeout choice is a freshness-vs-cost trade-off — a longer interval widens the stale-data window before a dead instance is caught, a shorter interval shrinks that window but multiplies check load — and since there's no universally correct number (it has to tie to the service's own SLO), a sane default is an interval around 10 seconds or under, tightened for a latency-sensitive service and loosened for a cheap, high-fan-out one.

Deregister only covers a graceful exit — it cannot save you from an instance that dies abruptly (OOM-killed, or the whole node disappearing) — so the calling side needs retry plus a circuit breaker as defense in depth, so a request landing on a not-yet-detected-dead instance fails fast and gets routed elsewhere instead of hanging or cascading.
The registry is only as fresh as its health-check cycle, so an abrupt death always leaves a stale entry until the next check fails.
During exactly that window, a consumer keeps getting routed to the dead address and hits connection refused.
Lever one: for planned stops, hook deregister into SIGTERM (orchestrators always give a grace period) so the instance leaves the catalog instantly.
Lever two: for abrupt death (OOM, node loss) you can't deregister at all, so you shorten the health-check Interval to shrink the stale-data window — traded against extra check load.
Make the consumer resilient with retry + circuit breaker, always reading only instances currently in the passing state.
The missing hour is not a bug in the app — it is the push transport's design surfacing under stress.
A push-based transport buffers outgoing lines in memory before shipping to the backend, and while the backend is briefly unreachable that buffer absorbs the backlog.

Once the outage outlasts the buffer's capacity, new lines are simply dropped — no exception, no crash — because the very path that would report the failure (the transport itself) is the one that is broken, so it silently swallows its own failure.
That is exactly why the app looked healthy the whole time — the failure was invisible from inside the app itself.
The fix is layering independence into the pipeline, not patching one spot.

Always run a console/stdout transport alongside the push transport, so the container engine (Docker/Kubernetes) keeps capturing every line out-of-band regardless of whether the backend push succeeds — a console transport on Node, a console sink on .NET, a console appender on Java, or writing straight to stdout on Go all do this.

Better still, decouple the app from the backend entirely: run a log-shipping agent (Promtail or Vector) as a sidecar that tails stdout and forwards it, so the app never depends on the backend's address or uptime at all and an outage there can't touch it.

Because this failure mode is silent by nature, add a monitor on ingestion rate, or a gap alert on the pipeline itself, so a future outage surfaces within minutes instead of a missing hour discovered by chance.
Metrics and logs can only tell you "it's slow," never "where," because neither preserves the causal path of one specific request.

Metrics are aggregates over time — great for reading overall rates and quantiles, but structurally blind to which hop in the call chain is the culprit; a single p95 number carries no information about the service behind it.

Logs are discrete events with no tree relationship to each other, so you cannot reassemble one request's journey across services from lines scattered independently across each service — no log line knows who its "parent" is.

A trace closes exactly that gap: it ties the request's steps into a tree under one traceId, each span carrying its own duration, so you read the timeline directly and see exactly which hop is stretching the latency.
This is the third pillar — causality over time — complementing metrics and logs, not replacing them.
"Must be the network" is precisely the unverified guess that a trace turns into actual evidence.
